newsitem.title: GERMANY: German chemical sector expects pay talk marathon.
newsitem.headline: German chemical sector expects pay talk marathon.

text.p: Germany's chemical sector, which earlier this year agreed a landmark 1996 wage pact linking a modest pay rise to job creation, was on Monday braced for the next round in altogether tougher 1997 wage talks.

Negotiations for next year's wage claim, which would normally be held next spring, have been brought forward because of huge resistance by workers to a new federal law allowing employers to make cuts in sick pay entitlements.

The new round of talks, scheduled to take place in a hotel outside Frankfurt on Tuesday, follow the failure of two earlier attempts to find a compromise on the sick pay cuts, which employers want to implement to reduce labour-related costs.
But even if agreement can be reached there, employers and union leaders have to bridge wide differences of opinion on what the wider 1997 wage increase should be.
"We've got some tough talks ahead of us," one party involved in the talks said on Monday.
Negotiations for the some 590,000 workers in the industry had been postponed until next January after the two earlier rounds collapsed on the issue of sick pay.

But following break-through agreements signed by metal and engineering employers last week that guaranteed workers full sick pay agreements, the IG Chemie trade union said that chemical employers were now ready to come back to the table.
The union said the BAVC chemical employers federation was now ready to accept full sick pay under certain conditions, a development that BAVC has not confirmed.
BAVC officials said on Monday they had not changed their position and still sought to reduce costs associated with long-term sickness as well as other labour-related costs.

Sick pay is however only one issue on which agreement must be reached. IG Chemie has already rejected an offer by employers of a 2.5 percent wage rise as "completely unacceptable", demanding a 4.2 percent increase.

That is far in excess of the two percent wage increase agreed for 1996 by workers in return for a pledge by employers to halt job cuts and introduce a series of measures to create 25,000 new jobs this year.
Moreover, the talks are unlikely to benefit from any the mutual understanding that has characterised past meetings between chemical workers and employers.
Relations in the sector have been soured by BASF AG's unsuccessful attempt in October to enforce the sick pay cuts, a decision it later reversed after walk-outs involving some 13,000 of its workers.

More widely, labour relations across Germany have been damaged by the collapse of a so-called "Alliance for Jobs" agreement involving unions, employers and government under which unions were to demand modest wage increases in return for measures to protect jobs and solve unemployment.

The alliance fell apart earlier this year as it became clear that the Bonn government was moving ahead with a cost-cutting budget that unions said only exacerbated the jobless problem and undermined the social state.
